title: A registry of runtime CLASSES, the vocabulary of what a runtime may be claimed to do, and the protocol every descriptor carries
description:
One document, three lists, and the same rule holds all three: nothing here may be written in any vendor's vocabulary. A CLASS states what is true of a runtime AS A KIND -- how an agent reaches it at all, and which translation sits in the gap -- so it can be shipped to a host running a tool that did not exist when this was written. A tool's proper name is never a class: the name of a product is the one thing about a runtime that is guaranteed not to be true of the kind, and a registry that carried one would have to be edited every time a vendor shipped.

The CAPABILITY vocabulary is the second list, and it is the one that makes an absence countable. A descriptor may only claim a capability this vocabulary declares, so the set of things a runtime has NOT claimed is enumerable -- which is the whole point: an unclaimed capability must be a gap with a NAME, and a name it can only have if somebody declared the word first. An empty list of claims reads as `none needed`; a vocabulary read against an empty list of claims reads as `six declared, none claimed`, and only the second is a measurement.

The PROTOCOL is the set of lines every descriptor carries whatever its class, declared once here so that they are RENDERED into each rather than restated in any. A host may add lines and may not edit these.

This shape is declared by the kit and authored by the host in exactly the same words: a class the kit never anticipated is declared by the host in a registry of its own rather than as a second kind of document. Two sources, one grammar.

protocol.description: The binding lines every descriptor carries, whichever class it composes. Declared once, projected into all -- a line that is rendered cannot be restated, and a line that cannot be restated cannot drift. The word is the composer's, not this subject's: what binds every composition of a kind is called a protocol wherever this kit composes anything, and a second word for it here would be a second home for one idea.

capabilities.description: Every capability a runtime may be claimed to have, named once so that both a claim and the ABSENCE of a claim have a word. A capability is declared here as a QUESTION -- what would have to be observed for this to be true -- and never as an answer about any particular tool.

means.description: What is being claimed, in one sentence, in the field's vocabulary and no vendor's.

observed_by.description: What would have to HAPPEN for this to stop being a claim. Declared beside the capability rather than left to whoever gets around to checking, because a capability whose proof nobody specified is proven by consensus -- which is testimony wearing a lab coat.

reach.description: How an agent reaches a runtime of this kind at all -- the one sentence that distinguishes it from every other kind. Not a feature list: features are claimed per instance and proven per instance.

boundary.description: The translation that sits in the gap for runtimes of this kind -- paths, quoting, encodings, clocks, line endings. Declared at the class because it is a property of the KIND of gap, and declared at all because this is the failure that does not announce itself: two components agree on a NAME, disagree on the REFERENT, and each behaves correctly while the work lands somewhere nobody chose.

reference_class.description: The field's own proven exemplars of this kind of boundary, named so that a descriptor is benchmarked rather than merely described. Standards and mechanisms, never products.
